newsitem.title: UK: AIDS drug shows promise against hepatitis.
newsitem.headline: AIDS drug shows promise against hepatitis.

text.p: Pharmaceuticals giant Glaxo Wellcome said on Thursday a drug originally developed for use against the HIV virus that causes AIDS had shown promising results against hepatitis.
Glaxo said its drug lamivudine worked well in clinical trials with patients who had severe liver disease caused by hepatitis B.
Lamivudine, also known as 3TC, is already sold for use against AIDS under the brand name Epivir.
Glaxo said its hepatitis study involved 358 Asian patients with chronic hepatitis B in Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan.

"These results indicate that over a one-year period, improvements in liver histology were demonstrated in a significantly higher percentage of lamivudine patients compared to placebo," the company said in a statement.

Lamivudine was developed by BioChem Pharma Inc. in Canada and was licensed to Glaxo in 1990. "Today's results from this phase III study, conducted in a clearly difficult-to-treat group of patients, support lamivudine's potential as a powerful new anti-viral therapy for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection," said Gervais Dionne, executive vice president of BioChem.
Analysts' estimates on the drug's sales prospects vary widely, ranging from a potential 200 million pounds ($324.6 million) a year to more than one billion pounds ($1.62 billion).
But they say it will be hard to market lamivudine as only two percent of hepatitis B sufferers live in the developed world.
"From a scientific point of view this is a very exciting prospect. In commercial terms there remain questions on its sale prospects," said one analyst.
The World Health Organisation estimates that around 350 million people carry the hepatitis B virus worldwide.
Hepatitis B is 100 times more infectious than HIV and can lead to severe liver scarring. It is responsible for 80 percent of cases of liver cancer.
